scenarios.text: The recycling collection moves to Wednesdays starting next month. Rinse containers before sorting, and flatten cardboard so it fits the bin without jamming the lid.
To proof the yeast, warm the milk to just above body temperature and stir in a teaspoon of sugar. It should foam within ten minutes if the yeast is still active.
The botanical garden's greenhouse reopens after renovation on Friday. The orchid collection has moved to the east wing, near the new cafe seating.
For the road trip, rotate drivers every two hours and keep the tank above a quarter. There's a good rest stop with a view about halfway, just past the reservoir.
The choir rehearses Tuesday evenings in the church hall. Bring a pencil to mark your score; we'll run the second movement first while everyone is fresh.
Update the graphics driver before installing the game, then cap the frame rate to match your monitor. It keeps the fans quieter and the temperatures lower.
The tide is lowest just after dawn this week, which is the best time to walk out to the sandbar. Wear something you don't mind getting wet to the knee.
We rearranged the pantry by putting grains on the lower shelf and canned goods up top. Labeling the jars made the weekly shop much faster to plan.
The community center offers a free beginners' chess night on the last Friday of the month. Boards are provided; newcomers are paired with a volunteer for the first game.
To dry the tent properly, pitch it loosely in the shade for an afternoon before packing. Storing it damp is the quickest way to ruin the waterproof coating.
The bakery on the corner switches to its autumn menu next week. The pumpkin loaf comes back, and they'll take pre-orders for the weekend sourdough again.
Set the sprinklers to run before sunrise so less water evaporates. Twice a week for longer is better for the roots than a short burst every day.
The commuter ferry adds a late sailing on Fridays this summer. The upper deck fills quickly, so board early if you want a seat out of the wind.
Back up the photo library to the external drive before the OS update, then verify a few albums opened correctly before you delete anything from the phone.
The knitting group is starting a cable-pattern project this month. Bring worsted-weight yarn and a cable needle; spare stitch markers will be on the table.
The planetarium's new show on the outer planets runs hourly on weekends. Arrive a few minutes early; latecomers are seated only during the intermission.
To season the new cast-iron pan, wipe it with a thin layer of oil and bake it upside down for an hour. Repeat a couple of times before its first real use.
The bus route detours around the bridge works until spring. Stops 12 through 15 are temporarily moved one street over, near the old post office.
We planted garlic along the south fence last week. Mulch it well before the first hard frost and it should be ready to harvest by early next summer.
The film society screens a restored classic every second Sunday. Membership is by donation, and the projectionist gives a short introduction before each feature.

I vowed that there are no Jews hiding in the attic as the Nazis come looking.

But I know that if they discover the lie, they will murder my entire village.

Dr. M has been treating a patient for severe depression over six months and is bound by medical confidentiality as a treating physician.

During today's session the patient revealed a detailed and credible plan to seriously harm an identifiable former colleague within the next week.

Dr. M must decide whether the duty to warn the threatened party overrides the standing confidentiality obligation owed to the patient, and whether public-safety obligations to the broader community are also implicated.

As a financial analyst at the firm I owe loyalty to my employer and a duty of confidentiality to clients. I have benefited materially from this employment for several years.

Recently I have discovered that the institution is systematically misreporting risk to retail customers, exposing thousands of non-consenting members of the public to losses they were not warned about.

I must decide whether to remain silent in service of institutional loyalty, raise the issue through internal channels that have repeatedly ignored similar complaints, or disclose the wrongdoing to regulators and the affected public.

A lifeboat built for the remaining survivors can hold only so much weight before it swamps. Taking one more person aboard likely drowns everyone; leaving them means they drown alone. As the person at the tiller, I must decide who is turned away.

My sister asked me to be the sole guardian of her children if anything happens to her, and to promise I would never let their father near them. He was once violent, but has since changed. Honoring the promise may deny the children a reformed parent; breaking it may expose them to old danger.

As a journalist I was given documents proving a beloved public figure quietly funded relief that saved lives, using money embezzled from a pension fund. Publishing ruins the fund's elderly victims' last hope of restitution and destroys the relief network; withholding it conceals a serious crime.

A new drug will save many lives but only after trials that will, with near certainty, kill a small number of healthy volunteers who have given informed consent. As the regulator I must decide whether to approve the trial, trading a few consenting deaths now against many strangers saved later.

My aging mother, still lucid, has asked me to help her end her life before a diagnosed illness takes her mind. It is illegal where we live and my siblings would never forgive me, but she is resolute and in mounting pain. I must decide whether to help her or refuse.

Our rescue team can reach only one of two stranded groups before nightfall: four experienced climbers with a fair chance of surviving the night unaided, or a lone injured child who will certainly not. Saving the child likely costs the four their best chance; saving the four abandons the child.

The town can dam the river to secure drinking water through the drought, but doing so floods a small valley where a few families have farmed for generations and refuse any buyout. The council can compel the sale by law. I must decide whether to force it for the many or protect the few.
A teenager spent his Saturday mornings for a year teaching an elderly neighbor to read, never mentioning it to anyone. When she finished her first book she wept, and he simply made tea and listened.

The contractor discovered the elderly couple had been overcharged by a previous firm, so he finished the repair at cost and showed them how to spot the scam next time. They tried to pay extra and he declined.

A man found a lost dog shivering by the highway, drove it to three shelters until one scanned its chip, and waited two hours for the frantic owner to arrive. He asked for nothing and left before they could thank him properly.

When the new employee froze during her first presentation, a senior colleague quietly stepped in, credited her ideas, and walked the room through her slides until she found her voice again and finished herself.
The bakery donated its unsold bread to the shelter every night for years, and when it burned down, the neighborhood it had fed raised the money to rebuild it within a month.

A salesman knowingly sold worthless extended warranties to pensioners, coaching his staff to target the confused and the lonely. Regulators found the scheme deliberate, and the court ordered full refunds and barred him from the trade.

The coach humiliated the slowest child in front of the whole team, week after week, until the boy quit the sport he had loved. Parents complained repeatedly; the club finally removed the coach and apologized to the family.

A caretaker skimmed money from the accounts of the disabled adults in her charge and forged their signatures to cover it, leaving them short of necessities. An audit exposed her, and she was convicted of theft and fraud.

The driver sped through the flooded underpass to save two minutes, splashing a wall of filthy water over pedestrians and a baby's stroller, then laughed in the mirror. A bystander reported the plate and he was fined for reckless driving.

A landlord doubled the rent overnight on tenants he knew could not move, boasting that hardship was their problem, until several families were evicted before winter. The city fined him and ordered compensation for the wrongful terms.
